reason: The narrative of Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16) fundamentally validates the divinely-established authority of Moses and Aaron against their challengers. Korah and his followers—the 'regular people' in revolt—challenge the leaders with the argument that 'all the congregation are holy' and question why Moses and Aaron exalt themselves (v. 3). God's response is unambiguous: the earth swallows the rebels alive, fire consumes the 250 men offering incense, and these events explicitly vindicate Moses's authority ('by this you shall know that the Lord has sent me,' v. 28). While the congregation later complains against the leaders (v. 41), they do so based on a fundamental misunderstanding of the events, and God again validates Moses and Aaron by commanding their separation to avoid collective destruction. The story's trajectory and divine judgment consistently demonstrate that the leaders are acting legitimately according to God's will, while those who oppose them—whether Korah's inner circle or the broader congregation that follows them—are portrayed as in error.
